newsitem.title: CHINA: Canada signs $3 billion nuclear deal with China.
newsitem.headline: Canada signs $3 billion nuclear deal with China.

text.p: Canada and China signed their biggest single commercial contract Tuesday, a $3 billion deal for the construction of two nuclear reactors that Ottawa hopes will be the first in a series of such orders, Canadian officials said.

Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. and China National Nuclear Corp. signed the contract for two 700-megawatt CANDU-6 nuclear reactors worth $2.99 billion (C$4 billion), to be built at Qinshan, Zhejiang province, about 50 miles from Shanghai.

The project will also involve partners from Japan, the United States and South Korea and will be co-financed by the national export credit agencies of the other partner countries, the Canadian consulate said.
Chinese Premier Li Peng and Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien witnessed the signing ceremony at a hotel outside Shanghai, Canadian officials said.

"It is Canada's hope that this contract will mark the beginning of a long-term commercial relationship between Canada and China in the peaceful and safe use of nuclear energy," Chretien said in prepared remarks.

Chretien flew to Shanghai Tuesday morning for a six-hour visit to attend the signing ceremony. He arrived from Manila, where he attended the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and was due to fly on to Japan.
The Canadian consulate said the deal would generate an estimated 27,000 direct and indirect person-years of employment in Canada over the six-year construction period.
Export Development Corp. of Canada would provide financing for the Canadian component of the sale, worth about $1.12 billion, or about C$1.5 billion, the statement said.
A Canadian diplomat said Tuesday's signing was the last link in a chain that began in November 1994 with a bilateral agreement between Chretien and Li.
"Over the last six months there have been very tight negotiations on terms and conditions," he said, comparing it to a long courtship culminating in Tuesday's wedding ceremony.

Kenneth Courtis, chief economist of Deutsche Bank Capital Markets (Asia) Ltd, said that nuclear energy markets in Europe and the United States were in decline and Japan's was largely closed to outsiders, making countries in the rest of Asia, as net importers of energy, the big market of the future.

"This agreement opens the possibility for eight more sales (to China), so that would potentially mean five times as much as this first transaction," he said in an interview in Shanghai. "The Chinese are very happy with the technology."
What drove future sales was the availability of low-cost credit to help the Chinese buy and the ability of the Chinese to build the plants and integrate them into their system, he said.

Courtis said that domestic opposition in Canada would not derail future sales in a country eager for export opportunities and high-paying jobs, with unemployment at about 10 percent and very slow economic growth.

In Ottawa, the ecology groups Sierra Club of Canada and Energy Probe said Monday they would sue the government over the reactor sales, charging it with violating its own environmental laws to promote the interests of the nuclear industry.
